summary:
Perm Krai, a federal subject of Russia, stands under the national framework documented by the UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025): same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections apply. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law barring gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed, and the expanded 'propaganda' law criminalises public expression that 'justifies' gender transition. That law carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to four years in prison.

The Supreme Court of Russia designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation in 2023. Participation carries 2 to 6 years' imprisonment and organising 6 to 10 years. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 convictions tied to the designation as of 30 June 2025. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation — one died by suicide in pretrial detention and courts sentenced two to prison — while 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols.

Foreigners who breach these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The speed of the post-designation crackdown was recorded by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented in the sources. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman known as 'Ada' was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Enforcement is expanding in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two preceding years. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life through 2025, including a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as 'a second-class citizen' after the designation.

No enforcement record specific to Perm Krai appears in the sources, so the region is assessed against the national pattern rather than as a separate regime. Survey data cited in the UK Home Office note show respondents in the Volga area, which includes Perm Krai, were more 'closeted' toward relatives than the whole-study sample. The same note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims; Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.
tangentialFactors:
The national position is reinforced by external advisories rather than regional variation: the US State Department rates Russia Level 4, Do Not Travel, and Human Rights Watch used its 30 June 2025 report to urge governments to provide safe haven to people leaving the country. A visitor leaving Perm Krai therefore faces the same exposure at the border and in transit as one departing any other part of Russia.

Enforcement turbulence is concentrated in the largest cities but is not confined to them. The Guardian's 17 January 2024 account of bar raids in Moscow within 48 hours of the extremist designation, and the Moscow Times reporting of 23 June 2025 on arrests, club raids and extremism charges, describe a nationwide post-designation campaign. Chechnya is identified in the UK Home Office note as a more severe pocket within the same national framework, cited there to support the refugee-convention assessment rather than as a separate legal order.

The conversion-therapy detention reported by BBC Russian on 27 July 2024 occurred near Novosibirsk and is used here as evidence of documented physical coercion against transgender people under the national framework, not as a Perm Krai incident. The death in pretrial detention reported by the Associated Press in December 2024 likewise concerns an extremism defendant held elsewhere.
localsOnly:
Residents of Perm Krai face the same criminal and administrative exposure as elsewhere in Russia: 2 to 6 years for participating in the designated extremist organisation and 6 to 10 for organising it, with up to 12 years available on the more serious participation charges, plus administrative liability under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and courts issued 101 extremism convictions tied to the 2023 designation by 30 June 2025. Residents who encounter police over symbols or online content risk detention and a criminal record that follows them.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: the 2023 law prohibits gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, and gender-affirming care is banned. There is no route to a corrected passport or other identity document, and same-sex marriage is not recognised, so partners have no marital standing. No statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation applies.

The UK Home Office note treats LGBT+ people in Russia, including Chechnya, as a particular social group under the refugee convention, which governs UK asylum claims; survey data cited in the note indicate that respondents in the Volga area were more 'closeted' toward relatives than the study sample as a whole.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Perm Krai-specific enforcement data — raids, prosecutions, detentions or regional measures on propaganda or public order — appears in the source inventory, and none is asserted here. Whether the regional administration has adopted measures beyond the national statutes is not sourced.

The eighteenfold growth in propaganda cases and the 60 million ruble fine total reported by Meduza on 19 June 2025 are national figures and are not disaggregated by federal subject; their distribution across Perm Krai is unresolved.

The inventory's two current sources carry different dates: the UK Home Office note is dated June 2025 with its assessment updated 11 June 2025, while a page-level update date of 12 August 2026 appears in the material. Which of those dates governs the currency of the baseline is not resolved here.

The Moscow Times material of 23 June 2025 is cited for the national pattern of arrests, raids and extremism charges; only one named local account (St Petersburg) is drawn from it, and no further regional breakdown was available.
